case_info.scenario: A man in his 50s presented with bleeding wounds and nodules on the bilateral hips and forearms. He previously received failed systemic and radiation therapy for tumor stage mycosis fungoides (MF). He had received 11 courses of extended beam radiation therapy, including 3 courses of total skin irradiation of 24 to 30 Gy, and focal irradiation to the left posterior thigh and hip/buttock with 2.5/3 Gy to 12.5/24 Gy, respectively, and the right posterior thigh and hip with 2 Gy to 20 and 26 Gy, respectively. Seven years before this visit, he underwent a reduced-intensity, matched, unrelated donor, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT). His post-transplant course was complicated by severe chronic graft vs host disease of the skin, eyes, and gut, for which he received systemic corticosteroid therapy, tacrolimus, methotrexate, and long-term extracorporeal photopheresis. Three years after the HSCT, he developed chronic ulcerations on the hips, back, and arms at the site of previously irradiated tumors, as well as multiple friable, hemorrhagic, and bleeding nodules on bilateral hips and his forearms while receiving treatment with corticosteroids and extracorporeal photopheresis. He underwent several debulking procedures and excision biopsies of the nodules, which revealed granulation tissue on histology. In this latest visit, physical examination revealed recurrent hemorrhagic and friable nodules on his left lateral hip and left lateral buttock (Figure 1). Similar nodules were noted on his right hip and forearm. The patient underwent repeated debulking and biopsy. He was also treated with micafungin, amphotericin B, levofloxacin, dapsone, acyclovir, pentamidine, penicillin VK, and posaconazole. Positron emission tomography (PET) computed tomography (CT) results did not show evidence of visceral or extracutaneous disease.
case_info.caption: Recurrent hemorrhagic and friable nodules on the left lateral hip.
case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.

Seven years before this visit, he underwent a reduced-intensity, matched, unrelated donor, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT). His post-transplant course was complicated by severe chronic graft vs host disease of the skin, eyes, and gut, for which he received systemic corticosteroid therapy, tacrolimus, methotrexate, and long-term extracorporeal photopheresis. Three years after the HSCT, he developed chronic ulcerations on the hips, back, and arms at the site of previously irradiated tumors, as well as multiple friable, hemorrhagic, and bleeding nodules on bilateral hips and his forearms while receiving treatment with corticosteroids and extracorporeal photopheresis. case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.

case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.

1. Mental Demand

   Scoring:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an

   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.

case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. case_info.explanation: A male in his 50s with a history of MF, radiation, allogeneic HSCT, chronic immunosuppression, and chronic graft vs host disease underwent multiple deep excision biopsies of various, recurrent chronic, hemorrhagic nodules at sites of previous radiation. Previous biopsies demonstrated granulation tissue. Histopathology of the specimen from the left hip, but not other sites, revealed an atypical vascular proliferation that was consistent with angiosarcoma (Figure 2). While PET-CT results did not show evidence of visceral metastatic disease, there was evidence of intensely hypermetabolic soft tissue along the anterolateral margins of the hips bilaterally, as well as skin thickening along the anterior abdominal wall with mild metabolic activity. Angiosarcoma was seen on only 1 biopsy specimen, and a multifocal presentation of secondary angiosarcoma would be unusual. However, given his history and presentation, as well as the limitations of coverage of PET imaging, the possibility of multiple site involvement was still considered. Surgical intervention was deemed suboptimal due to poor definition of the true margins of the neoplasm and anticipated poor wound healing of the previously irradiated area. He was treated with 4 cycles of paclitaxel, and evaluation of response was difficult due to the admixed granulation tissue. Results from PET-CT showed no evidence of disease progression 4 months later, so further treatment with chemotherapy was discontinued. Angiosarcoma is a rare tumor, comprising only 2% of soft tissue sarcomas, with an incidence of 2 to 5 cases per 1 000 000 annually.1It is associated with poor prognosis, high rates of local recurrence, and metastasis.2The tumor originates from vascular endothelial cells, which grow along channels and sinusoidal and cavernous spaces; organize into vessels, masses, or nodules3; and can occur in most organs. On histopathology, they can be difficult to diagnose given some similarity with other vascular tumors3; however, the presence of dissecting growth pattern, protrusion of atypical cells into vascular lumens, and atypical cytomorphologic features of the lining are helpful features in differentiating angiosarcoma from other vascular tumors. They are more prevalent in men at a median age of 60 years. The cutaneous form is more common in elderly White men.4To our knowledge, it has not been described in association with allogeneic HSCT or MF previously. The skin is the most commonly involved organ, predominantly on the head and neck.3Chronic lymphedema and radiation therapy are primary risk factors, along with familial syndromes, environmental chemical toxins, and foreign bodies.4Radiation therapy contributes to one-fourth of all cases.3Immunosuppression may be a risk factor, although the effect is unknown, as angiosarcomas have been reported in kidney transplant patients who have subsequent immunosuppression.5 Treatment usually requires a multidisciplinary approach, but the recurrence rate remains high. Surgical resection and therapeutic agents, such as cytotoxic therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy, have been applied. Data are lacking regarding best treatment plans because angiosarcoma is so rare and much of the literature exists in case reports.6 The diagnosis of angiosarcoma can be difficult to establish, as initial presentation can be mistaken for a bruise or hemangioma, and delays in diagnosis have been previously reported with a median of 5.1 months.7As the tumor grows, further cutaneous signs may develop with tissue infiltration, edema, ulceration, and hemorrhage.4Repeated evaluation is key when there is clinical suspicion of malignant transformation. In this article, we presented a case of a patient who developed a cutaneous angiosarcoma in the setting of a known history of chronic graft vs host disease following receipt of radiation to the sites to treat his underlying MF, ablative therapy for bone marrow transplant, and subsequent immunosuppression.
